Formulation
- Brief summary:
  - Young adult female with recent onset (2–3 days) of constant lower central abdominal ache associated with nausea and hot/sweaty feelings. She reports recent constipation (~1 week ago) which has since improved and increased urinary frequency (drinks a lot of water) without dysuria or urgency. She has an Implanon contraceptive implant and reports light pink discoloration observed in urine/possible spotting in the days prior to expected menses (last menstrual period ~3+ weeks ago). Key precipitating factors appear to be recent bowel disturbance; pregnancy and other causes were appropriately considered by clinician and planned to be excluded. Protective/social supports include living with boyfriend and active engagement in care. No psychiatric history or current mental health symptoms were elicited.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute lower abdominal pain with nausea (physical presentation)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Attend in-person GP assessment today; obtain clarification/exclusion of pregnancy and cause of abdominal pain; return to usual health.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Perform face-to-face clinical examination and appropriate investigations to exclude pregnancy and other causes of lower abdominal pain; provide diagnosis and management plan.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend agreed face-to-face GP appointment (patient agreed to make time; clinician requested ideally today).
  - Seek urgent care if symptoms worsen (light-headedness, fainting, increasing pain, vomiting, fever, or other concerning changes).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - See patient face-to-face for physical examination.
  - Arrange pregnancy testing and any further investigations deemed appropriate based on clinical examination (as discussed by clinician).
  - Provide urgent advice and arrange escalation if examination/investigations indicate need.

Secondary Problem: Possible intermenstrual bleeding/spotting or pink discoloration of urine
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Clarify source of pink discoloration and relation to menstrual cycle.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Determine whether spotting is menstrual, urinary, or other in origin; manage appropriately.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Report any increase in bleeding, vaginal discharge, or changes in symptoms at face-to-face visit or sooner if concerned.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Assess for vaginal discharge, perform appropriate pelvic/abdominal examination and pregnancy test; consider urine analysis if indicated.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Need for face-to-face assessment and testing (including pregnancy exclusion).
  - Advice to seek urgent care if symptoms worsen (light-headedness, fainting, increased pain, vomiting, fever, or other concerning changes).
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - New or worsening light-headedness, fainting, severe or increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, significant bleeding or other new concerning symptoms.
